clue.text: Dick placed between Ted and Hal!

definitions.text: Dick placed between Ted and Hal!

parts.words: Dick placed between Ted and Hal!
parts.note: Dick is a pet form of a royal name; Ted and Hal are pet forms of Edward and Henry, and this king reigned between Edward V and Henry VII

explanation.surface: Someone called Dick is seated at a party between two friends, Ted and Hal.
explanation.walkthrough: The casual nicknames hide English kings: Ted is Edward, Hal is Henry, and the king who came between the last Edward of York and the first Tudor Henry is the one meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkist monarch whose reign followed Edward V and preceded Henry VII, the last Plantagenet king of England.

clue.text: Make love?

parts.note: love is the tennis word for a score of zero, so making something love means bringing it down to zero

explanation.surface: A coy question about romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is amorous, but love here is the tennis score of nil, so 'make love' means turn into nil.
explanation.definitionFit: Love means zero in tennis scoring, so making something love is cutting it right down to zero, to nil.

clue.text: I entered dream-home-in Spain suitably enough

definitions.note: the answer is a region of Spain, which suits the Spanish idiom used for the wordplay

indicators.note: the letter I enters, going inside the word for a dream home

parts.note: a castle in Spain is an idiom for a daydream, an imaginary dream home

explanation.surface: Someone settles into their fantasy villa in Spain, which seems fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Castles in Spain' (or in the air) are idle dreams; the region of Spain clued is fittingly built from that castle.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic kingdom and region of central Spain, whose name the clue fittingly builds from a castle.

clue.text: Boy that is raised in France

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: cela is French for that, as the words in France tell us

explanation.surface: A lad who was brought up in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' says to take 'that' in French, CELA; 'raised' turns it upwards in this down answer to give ALEC.
explanation.definitionFit: Alec is a male first name, so it stands for a boy in crossword style.

clue.text: Fresh lies and disclaimers

indicators.note: fresh suggests a new version, so the letters of lies and are made anew

explanation.surface: Someone answers new falsehoods with a stream of denials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' tells you to remake LIES AND into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Disclaimers are statements refusing responsibility, the same as rejections or refusals of a claim.

clue.text: Pelt American all round ring? That's sickening

indicators.note: the pelt and the American go all round, enclosing the ring

parts.note: a pelt is an animal's skin, a hide
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: An American fur coat wrapped round a ring makes someone feel sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all round' means the two outer pieces wrap the ring between them; 'That's' is only a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sickening is revolting or ghastly to look at.

clue.text: It is found growing next to a trunk

definitions.text: It is found growing next to a trunk

parts.words: It is found growing next to a trunk
parts.note: sounds like a plant by a tree trunk, but the trunk is an elephant's nose, and an ivory tooth grows beside it

explanation.surface: Something like ivy or a fungus sprouts beside a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The trunk is not a tree's but an elephant's.
explanation.definitionFit: An elephant's long ivory tooth grows from the upper jaw just beside its long nose.

clue.text: Have something in mind

parts.note: read literally, to hold a picture in the mind rather than to intend something

explanation.surface: Someone is told they must have an idea or plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means to intend; read literally it is to form a picture in the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To picture or conceive something mentally is to form a mental image.

clue.text: Turn nasty in play

parts.note: a nasty situation is a dangerous one
a turn in the road is a corner

explanation.surface: A drama takes an ugly turn.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is a 1932 drama by J. B. Priestley.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage drama by J. B. Priestley about a dinner party where secrets come out.

clue.text: Pick out scattered cinders

indicators.note: scattered tells us the letters of cinders are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sifts through cinders thrown about by a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scattered' rearranges CINDERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To perceive or distinguish something is to make it out, to recognise it.

clue.text: It's said wildly in a row, to show contempt

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go in, inside the word for a row

parts.note: a din is a loud row or racket

indicators.note: wildly says the letters of said are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: An angry remark shouted in a quarrel expresses scorn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' and 'a' are links; 'wildly' signals the anagram and 'in' the container, and the definition is the verb phrase, with 'to' joining it.
explanation.definitionFit: To disdain is to treat with scorn, to look down on something.

clue.text: Slice the approach shot

definitions.meaning: a slice or sliver is a small piece cut off
in golf a short lofted shot onto the green

explanation.definitionFit: A small cut-off piece is a slice; in golf the short lofted approach to the green is also a chip shot.

clue.text: Food brought home

parts.note: alludes to the idiom about earning a living, literally food that a breadwinner brings home

explanation.surface: Someone carries groceries back to the house.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'bring home the bacon' is an idiom for earning a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Cured pork, the food in the idiom about earning money for the household.

clue.text: Churchwarden's hose

definitions.meaning: a churchwarden is a long-stemmed clay smoking ...; the 's is read as is
a hose is a tube for carrying water

explanation.surface: A church official's stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: A churchwarden is not the parish officer but a long clay tobacco pipe; hose is not stockings but a water tube.
explanation.definitionFit: A churchwarden is a type of long clay tobacco pipe, and a hose is a tube that carries water.

clue.text: Sue's going round the British Museum returning to board public transport

indicators.note: returning means the whole result is read backwards, upwards in this down entry
Sue goes round, enclosing the abbreviation for the museum

parts.note: the name Sue as written, 's being a link
BM is the standard abbreviation for the British Museum

explanation.surface: Sue tours the British Museum, then heads back to catch a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' gives SBMUE, and 'returning' turns that whole run upwards in this down entry; 'to' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To embus is to get on a bus or other vehicle, used chiefly of troops.

clue.text: Make a speech in the gutter

definitions.meaning: to hold forth at length, orate pompously
a drainpipe or lip that channels rainwater

explanation.surface: An orator ends up speaking from the gutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To declaim at length is to hold forth; a downpipe from a roof's rain gully is also so called.

clue.text: Yet it doesn't usually contain mother's ruin

definitions.text: Yet it doesn't usually contain mother's ruin

indicators.note: ruin tells us to wreck the letters of mother's into another order

explanation.surface: A flask is seldom used to carry gin, called mother's ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mother's ruin' is British slang for gin; here 'ruin' rearranges MOTHERS, and a vacuum flask seldom holds gin.
explanation.definitionFit: A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold, usually tea or soup rather than gin.

clue.text: C-in-C gets drink, gets more merry

parts.note: to sup is to drink

indicators.note: merry suggests tipsiness, so the letters of more are jumbled

explanation.surface: The commander-in-chief has a drink and gets jollier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'merry' gives REMO; both instances of 'gets' are simple links. C-in-C stands for commander-in-chief.
explanation.definitionFit: A commander-in-chief is the person in overall charge, a boss.

clue.text: Certainly bound to be different

indicators.note: the letters of bound to are made to be different, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a result is sure to change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be different' rearranges BOUND TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Indisputably, beyond question: an adverb of assurance.

clue.text: For certificate see master after swim

indicators.note: after means the other pieces follow the word for swim

parts.note: a dip is a short swim
lo is an old word meaning look or see
MA is a Master of Arts

explanation.surface: Someone gets a swimming certificate from their instructor after a dip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is a link; 'after swim' puts the swimming piece first, with the rest following it.
explanation.definitionFit: A document awarded on completing a course of study.

clue.text: Sells the dummy touchdowns possible

definitions.meaning: in rugby, to fake a pass; also attempts a deception
in rugby a try is a touchdown, and tries that are 'on' are possible

explanation.definitionFit: To attempt a deception is to try it on; and in rugby scores that are achievable can be said to be 'on'.

clue.text: Knocked out, so no cup tickets required

indicators.note: knocked out suggests a battered state, so the letters of so no cup are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A team is eliminated, so no tickets are needed for the cup final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked out' rearranges SO NO CUP; 'required' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Vouchers or slips exchanged for goods, in wartime rationing used like tickets.

clue.text: French writer and director of film company has acute difficulty

definitions.text: French writer and director of film

indicators.note: difficulty implies the letters of acute are in trouble, mixed up

explanation.surface: A French filmmaker's studio is in serious trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'difficulty' gives CTEAU; 'has' is a link. The definition covers both of his careers, poet and filmmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Cocteau was a French poet, novelist and filmmaker, maker of La Belle et la Bete.

clue.text: One may look better after visiting him

definitions.text: One may look better after visiting him

parts.words: One may look better after visiting him
parts.note: sounds like a beautician, but looking better means seeing better, after an eye examination

explanation.surface: A beauty specialist improves a client's appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look better' means see better, not appear more attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye doctor whose treatment or glasses improve a patient's sight.

clue.text: Wrinkles the ends

definitions.meaning: useful hints, as in tricks of the trade

explanation.definitionFit: Wrinkles are handy hints or pointers; ends of things are their points.

clue.text: Flog what might be silver

definitions.meaning: to beat with a cane or rod

explanation.definitionFit: To beat someone with twigs; also a tree, one kind called silver.

clue.text: Loud exchange in game

indicators.note: exchange means the letters of loud swap places

explanation.surface: A noisy argument breaks out during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchange' rearranges LOUD; the board game is a children's dice race.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple board game in which players race counters round by dice throws.

clue.text: Prison for a high-flier?

definitions.meaning: ..., from rhyming slang ...-lime for time, means a prison sentence

explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a jail term, from rhyming slang bird-lime for time; and a flying creature.

clue.text: Childishly claims the luggage

definitions.meaning: children shout this to claim something first

explanation.definitionFit: Children say it to stake a claim on something; cases and suitcases are also called this.

clue.text: Playfully tickled, they supply notes

parts.note: tickling the keys is slang for playing piano, and the keys were once made of elephant tusk

explanation.surface: Something giggles when tickled and passes on messages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tickle the ivories' is an idiom for playing the piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano keys, once made from elephant tusk, produce the musical notes when pressed.

clue.text: Delight in story-telling, right from the start

indicators.note: from the start says the letter goes from the very beginning of the word

parts.note: relation is the act of telling a story

explanation.surface: Someone takes pleasure in telling stories from the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R from the start of RELATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Great happiness and exhilaration, a joyful state.

clue.text: A great one for asking questions

definitions.text: A great one for asking questions

parts.words: A great one for asking questions
parts.note: sounds like a nosy person, but read as a chief questioner, the head of the Spanish Inquisition

explanation.surface: Someone who is very curious and always asking things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great' hints at grand, and the 'one asking questions' is an inquisitor: the head of the Inquisition.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of the Spanish Inquisition, chief examiner of suspected heretics, such as Torquemada.
